item.title: From the gridiron to greatness: SU alum's film earns festival selection
item.description: After spending nearly two decades playing football, Glenn Brown III is pursuing a different creative path. The 2023 Southern University and A&M College graduate is now making his mark as a filmmaker, with his psychological thriller, "You Should’ve Looked Closer," selected for the 37th New Orleans Film Festival. For Brown, the transition from athletics to filmmaking is about more than changing careers. It is about challenging expectations and finding an identity beyond the sport that shaped much of his life. “I knew sports was something that I was good at. I knew it wasn’t who I was,” Brown said. Courtesy: glennabrowniii/Instagram   Brown grew up in Lutcher, LA and began playing football since he was five years old, including his time as a four-year starter at Southern as a defensive back. He said moving on from a sport that had occupied so much of his life was not easy. “It’s hard to focus on something for almost 20 years, and then just move on from it,” Brown said. “That’s hard. People don’t mention that enough.” He also recognized how expectations can shape the paths athletes believe are available to them, particularly Black athletes. “As an athlete with our skin color, they want to put you in a box, like you’re an athlete. That’s all you are and that’s all you’re going to be,” Brown said. “If you don’t make it to the NFL, you’re going to be a coach and I just wasn’t going for that.” Rather than limit himself to the future others might have expected, Brown looked to entertainers and filmmakers who had successfully moved between creative fields. He cited Ice Cube’s transition from music to filmmaking and acting, along with Will Smith’s career in television and film, as examples that inspired him. Brown also connected with the journey of filmmaker Ryan Coogler, who played football before pursuing a career in film, and actor LaKeith Stanfield, whom Brown worked alongside as a stand-in on the film "I Love Boosters." Courtesy: Glenn Brown III Finding his voice through film Brown’s interest in filmmaking began long before "You Should’ve Looked Closer." He said his father made films and music videos in New Orleans, while his grandmother regularly bought movies for the family to watch. Those early experiences helped develop his interest in storytelling. While at Southern, Brown studied mass communication with a focus in journalism. He initially wanted to pursue sports broadcasting, inspired by watching sports commentators, including Stephen A. Smith, Shannon Sharpe, Skip Bayless and Ryan Clark. Balancing academics with the demands of being a starting football player was challenging. Brown said he struggled in the classroom while focusing heavily on football and creating YouTube content. The possibility of becoming academically ineligible and losing his scholarship forced him to take his studies more seriously. He said the experience helped him develop the discipline and accountability he now relies on as a filmmaker. “I had to step into that role and learn how to direct myself, and hold myself accountable,” Brown said. Although he enjoys writing and acting more than directing, Brown took on multiple responsibilities to complete his first film. He wrote, directed, produced and acted in his film “You Should’ve Looked Closer.” Brown established his production company, Elephant Hill Media, in 2024 while studying acting at Catapult Studios in Atlanta. He said creating his own projects also gave him a way to keep working during periods when acting opportunities were limited. “I want to own something,” Brown said. “It’s just good to have ownership and, you know, build from the ground up.” A film about mental health and perception “You Should’ve Looked Closer” is an experimental psychological thriller centered on a young man named King. The film explores mortality, memory and perception through a nontraditional editing style that invites audiences to interpret what they see. Brown said he wanted to address suicide without depicting the act itself. Courtesy: Glenn Brown III/Elephant Hill Media The idea became meaningful to Brown when he wrote the film in the summer of 2025. He said several people in his hometown had taken their lives, including people connected to St. James High School, where he attended. Brown said he has long been drawn to stories that challenge audiences and spark conversations about uncomfortable subjects. With his first film, he wanted to explore the experiences of people coping with the loss of a loved one who struggled with their mental health. He also hopes the film encourages viewers who may be struggling to recognize that people around them care about them. Brown said he wants audiences to develop their own interpretations of the experimental film, while also considering the lives and relationships affected by suicide. Looking ahead When Brown submitted “You Should’ve Looked Closer” to film festivals, he did not expect it to be selected. He recalled receiving the notification while sitting in a barbershop and smiling as he processed the news. “I had no expectations at all,” he said. The selection gave Brown an opportunity to introduce his work to a wider audience as he continues developing his craft. He is now writing a feature-length supernatural horror film set in New Orleans. Brown hopes to secure at least $50,000 in funding to make the project and pay the people involved, with an emphasis on working with Louisiana talent. He also wants to tell stories that reflect the state beyond familiar stereotypes, exploring both its positive and difficult realities through a Black Southern Gothic perspective. “There just aren’t enough films about Louisiana,” Brown said. “I want to make a movie and make a film about Louisiana, the good parts and the bad parts, and have really uncomfortable conversations.” For Southern students pursuing interests outside their original career plans, Brown encourages them to take lessons from their education and apply them to whatever path they choose. “It’s always something you could take away from anything that you decide to study,” he said. “You Should’ve Looked Closer” is scheduled to screen Oct. 23 at 8 p.m. and Oct. 26 at 3 p.m. at the Contemporary Arts Center in New Orleans as part of the 37th New Orleans Film Festival. item.title: Southern University professor selected for 2026 Alex Trebek Legacy Fellowship
item.description: Darrell Roberson, co-director and chair of the digital media arts program and Title III activity director at Southern University and A&M College, has been selected for the 2026 Alex Trebek Legacy Fellowship. The fellowship, awarded by the Television Academy Foundation in Hollywood, California, supports educators from community colleges and minority-serving institutions in attending the foundation’s annual Media Educators Conference.  The three-day conference will take place Oct. 21-23 at the Television Academy’s North Hollywood campus, connecting college educators with television industry professionals through seminars on the art, science and business of television. “I’m honored to be one of 18 faculty members from universities around the country selected as a 2026 Alex Trebek Legacy Fellow and to represent Southern University,” Roberson said. “I look forward to bringing back ideas and connections that can help us build our program, prepare our students, and benefit the university.” Roberson and fellow co-director Harry Anderson Sr. lead Southern’s digital media arts program. The program is designed to equip students with both creative and technical skills, and combines hands-on production experience with a strong foundation in theory, humanities, and digital technologies. Roberson teaches video editing and sports production and helps develop the studios where students gain hands-on experience in digital media. This year, Roberson helped organize Southern’s inaugural Digital Media Arts Conference and second annual Digital Media Arts Symposium, bringing students together with working media professionals. Established in 2021 by the Harry & Judy Friedman Family Foundation, the Alex Trebek Legacy Fellowships honor the late Alex Trebek, longtime host of the television game show Jeopardy! The program provides financial support to educators seeking to enhance their teaching and strengthen connections between academic programs and the television industry.

item.title: Former Southern University professor tied to Nobel Prize-winning discovery
item.description: Southern University and A&M College professor emeritus Ali R. Fazely, Ph.D. has contributed to research connected to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the groundbreaking scientific project at the center of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. Fazely collaborated with Francis Halzen, Ph.D., a University of Wisconsin–Madison physicist who received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. The American Institute of Physics announced the recognition Oct. 6. Located at the South Pole, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory uses more than 5,000 optical sensors embedded in approximately one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice to detect faint flashes of light produced when neutrinos interact with matter. These nearly massless particles can travel vast distances through the universe, carrying information about some of its most energetic events. The discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources gave scientists a new way to study distant cosmic events beyond traditional observations using light. Fazely has led Southern’s IceCube-related research activities since 1997, working with graduate students, post-doctoral researchers and scientific collaborators. His team’s work has focused on detector simulations, rare particle decays, supernova neutrinos and high-energy neutrino interaction cross sections. Fazely said Southern’s participation in the international collaboration highlights the role historically Black colleges and universities can play in advancing scientific research. “Southern University's participation demonstrates that HBCUs can be active contributors to these efforts, not simply observers of discoveries made elsewhere,” said Fazely. Southern’s research has helped support the scientific work behind the observatory through computer simulations that model how neutrinos interact with matter, how charged particles travel through ice and how light reaches the detector’s optical sensors. These models help researchers interpret the signals IceCube records, reconstruct neutrino energies and directions, and assess potential improvements to the detector. The university’s research group has developed simulations for the existing IceCube detector, the IceCube Upgrade and the proposed IceCube-Gen2 observatory. Recent efforts have focused on supernova-neutrino simulations and future detector configurations that could help scientists identify astrophysical signals and investigate physical processes that have not yet been observed. Fazely’s research also includes studies of rare particle decays and high-energy neutrino interactions. A study exploring the possibility of observing the rare decay of an eta particle into a neutrino-antineutrino pair was published in Physical Review D in 2010. In 2019, the team published research in Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics introducing a Prime-Index parametrization of neutrino-nucleon and proton-proton cross sections. The research program has also created opportunities for Southern students to participate in advanced scientific investigations. Fazely said two students, Cheng Guo and Aaron Richard, completed Master of Science degrees through IceCube-related research, while graduate student Justin Mitchell is currently involved in the program. Through their involvement, students gain experience in particle physics, astrophysics, computer programming, statistical analysis and large-scale scientific simulations. They also become familiar with the research methods and scientific standards used in major international collaborations, preparing them for doctoral studies, research careers, national laboratories and technology-related professions. For Fazely, the program’s impact extends beyond scientific findings to the development of future researchers. “I am particularly proud that our program has combined scientific research with the education and mentoring of young scientists," he said. "In my view, that is one of Southern University's most important contributions to the future of physics.”

Southern University students create award-winning platform to support cancer patients
item.description: Courtesy of Nexus Louisiana Competing in DevDays for the first time, the team won with Tomorrow, a platform that helps patients protect their emotional well-being and sense of identity during treatment When a Southern University business professor forwarded Jha'Hannah Pink an email about DevDays, the timing was personal. Pink, an agribusiness major, had recently lost her uncle to cancer. He became the motivation behind Tomorrow, the cancer support platform she and her teammates built during the 10-week competition. Tomorrow won first place in the DevDays Cancer Care and Prevention Challenge in Southern University's first time competing in DevDays. The competition is a partnership between Nexus Louisiana and Ochsner Health that asked Louisiana college students to build technology to improve the cancer care experience for patients, caregivers and healthcare teams. "Tomorrow is about giving patients a reason to look forward to tomorrow," Pink said. "A lot of times, when you have all those treatments and appointments, you forget what you're living for and who you're living for. Our app is centered around helping patients remember that and helping them fight for tomorrow." Pink and her teammates, Thomas Reid and Jalayah Jones, study business and nursing. They earned $6,000 for the win. A platform built around quality of life Tomorrow is designed to work alongside hospital care. It helps patients keep their sense of identity, look after their emotional well-being and stay connected to the people and experiences that matter most during treatment. "I think healthcare does a good job at keeping them alive, but who is helping them harness that life inside of them, keep them positive, keep them happy?" Pink said. Patients get a personal profile where they can track their emotional wellness with hopeScore. They also receive encouraging reminders through tomorrowSpark and have access to an appointment calendar and AI-powered guidance. The platform includes Living Proof, a collection of survivor stories, along with wellness resources, cancer news and research, and a Legacy Vault where patients can save memories and life stories. The goal is to put quality of life alongside treatment, so patients remember not only what they are fighting against, but what they are fighting for. Building the app was the team's biggest hurdle. "We are not in computer science, so it was difficult trying to find a platform that incorporated everything that I wanted to have in it," Pink said. For Pink, the most valuable part of the experience was finally presenting the team's work to the judges. "I feel relieved. I'm happy," she said. "I think the judges and everyone kind of saw the vision." Multiple approaches to one challenge About 50 students from nine colleges and universities applied to compete in the challenge. Ten teams advanced to the finals, representing Southern University, Southeastern Louisiana University, the Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine, the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, the University of Louisiana at Monroe and Louisiana Tech University. Finalist teams presented their prototypes on Sept. 25 at Nexus Louisiana's Baton Rouge headquarters to a panel of healthcare, technology and business leaders. They competed for a share of $10,000 in cash prizes. Second place and $3,000 went to OncoReady from the University of Louisiana at Monroe. Computer science and engineering students Pankaj Bhatta, Jeevan Parajuli and Swabhiman Paudel developed a prototype to help care teams identify and address clinical and logistical barriers before a patient's scheduled cancer treatment. Third place and $1,000 went to Cancer Krewe from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. Computer science and engineering students Kaitlyn Damare, Ky Smith and Amaya Erhabor built a caregiver and treatment coordination web app that helps patients and their support circles organize appointments, delegate tasks and understand medical information. "Each team approached the same problem differently, showing the many ways technology can support patients and families," said Tony Zanders, president and CEO of Nexus Louisiana. "Tomorrow shows what can happen when students bring their personal experiences and skills to a real challenge. This is not just a project. There are real lives impacted by this technology." Ten weeks of development Over 10 weeks, student teams developed solutions focused on patient navigation, access to care, communication, remote monitoring and support. Judges evaluated each solution on its technical complexity, potential to scale and novelty. The judges were Dianne Teal, regional chief nursing director at Ochsner Health; Craig Davis, founder and CEO of Catalyze Labs; Trivia Frazier, biotech founder and CEO of Obatala Sciences; and Dr. Patrick Quinlan, founder and CEO of Hippo Technologies and former CEO of Ochsner Health. Ochsner Health brought clinical expertise and leadership to the challenge through Ochsner MD Anderson Cancer Center. "We have so many big problems to solve, and we're not going to solve them by continuing to do what we've always done," Teal said. "Having the fresh eyes of young people on how we're going to solve these things is so critical." The finals also featured remarks from Scott Mabry, chief operating officer of Ochsner Health Capital Region, and Eli Brodsky, deputy director of the Louisiana Department of Health. Brodsky discussed the state's investments to improve healthcare access in rural communities, including a new fund to support companies testing and scaling direct-to-patient technologies in rural Louisiana. Beyond the competition For Reid, DevDays turned into more than a shot at a cash prize. "I'm going to be honest, what got me into this project was the prize money," Reid said. "But hearing from the judges how we can take this from just a pitch, an idea, and really turn it into a business has me thinking way past this competition. We can actually make a real startup. I'm really thankful to Nexus for broadening our horizons and giving us an opportunity to do something we wouldn't have done without them." The team now plans to work toward bringing Tomorrow to market. As DevDays winners, they also automatically advance to the Nexus Technology Cup in December. DevDays is Nexus Louisiana's innovation competition that connects Louisiana college students with industry partners seeking new approaches to real operational and community challenges. Participants build functional solutions, receive expert feedback and present their work to potential employers, partners and investors. The Cancer Care and Prevention Challenge continues a partnership between Nexus Louisiana and Ochsner Health that previously challenged students to improve adolescent ACL injury prevention and recovery.

item.title: Southern University awarded $1.275 million to launch rural business center
item.description: Southern University and A&M College has received a $1.275 million, three-year cooperative agreement from the Minority Business Development Agency (MBDA) to establish the Louisiana Innovation for Thriving Rural Business (LIFT) Center, an initiative designed to strengthen rural businesses, expand access to financing and government contracting opportunities, and increase advanced manufacturing capabilities across Louisiana. Housed in the College of Business, the LIFT Center will provide eligible rural Louisiana businesses with coordinated access to business assessments, consulting, training and specialized assistance. Southern is one of only three historically Black colleges and universities in the country selected by MBDA to lead a Rural Business Center focused on advancing rural and manufacturing-based small businesses. The center will bring together expertise from the Southern University Law Center, the College of Sciences and Engineering, and Southern’s Advanced Metal Additive Manufacturing Laboratory. Through this collaboration, business owners will have access to resources designed to strengthen their operations, prepare for financing, pursue government contracting opportunities and expand their capacity to compete in advanced manufacturing industries. A signature hands-on manufacturing program will give entrepreneurs opportunities to explore businesses focused on making, repairing and testing metal parts for agriculture, energy and defense supply chains. Participants will pair advanced manufacturing expertise with business training to help transform technical skills into viable and sustainable enterprises. KDM & Associates LLC will lead program management and provide consulting in cybersecurity certification readiness, federal contracting, supplier development and manufacturing. Through the LIFT Center, Southern and its partners will work to expand the pool of contract-ready small and emerging businesses positioned to pursue opportunities with federal agencies, including the Small Business Administration, Department of War, Department of Energy, Department of Commerce, NASA, U.S. Department of Agriculture, U.S. Department of Education, Department of Housing and Urban Development, Department of the Interior and Department of Transportation. KDM’s digital platform also will provide virtual training, connect businesses with prospective partners and help monitor participant progress. Over the three-year award period, the LIFT Center aims to serve 500 clients, help 50 new businesses enter the federal supply chain, assist clients in securing $2.125 million in capital and support the creation of 600 jobs. The center will serve eligible rural Louisiana businesses through business assistance, entrepreneurial development and workforce training. These services are designed to expand access to markets, strengthen business capacity and support the long-term growth of Louisiana’s rural economy beyond the award period. Patrick Mensah, Formosa Endowed Professor of Mechanical Engineering and senior associate vice chancellor for academic affairs, will serve as principal investigator. Donald Andrews, professor and dean of the College of Business, will serve as co-principal investigator. Aloyce R. Kaliba, of the College of Business, will serve as project director, and Keith Moore of KDM & Associates will serve as collaborating program manager. Business owners seeking information about eligibility, services and upcoming activities may contact Mensah at patrick.mensah@sus.edu.

item.title: Entertainment or Avoidance
item.description: For many tourists looking to satiate their curiosities about spirituality, southern folklore, and supernatural, Louisiana is often a first choice. Every Halloween season, they seek the spooky sensations of ghosts in the French Quarter or haunted antebellum mansions. There exists a conflict, however, behind these festivities. When visitors view these locations and stories through a haunted or supernatural lens, does it honor the past or make guests more comfortable with an uncomfortable history? Turning plantations and other historical sites into profitable attractions is not a rare practice in Louisiana. Still, the approach doesn’t sit well with everyone. Taja Duplessis, a sophomore business management major from New Orleans, critiques the custom. “There’s a way to go about it,” she said. “It shouldn’t be a money‑making thing. You should be learning specifically about historical information.” That concern extends to how these sites are presented. Professor Latrenda Clark, a history and political science teacher at Southern University, explained that associating real history with ghosts and other supernatural beings provides observers with a buffer between fantasy and an upsetting reality. “A haunted house allows visitors to acknowledge terrible happenings without naming it within the system,” Clark said. “It’s a way to erase the victims of slavery and make it about the ghost story.” This buffer became increasingly visible at Nottoway Plantation in White Castle, Louisiana. The largest antebellum mansion in the South was destroyed by a fire in May of 2025. The mansion, built and maintained by more than 150 enslaved individuals, operated as a resort and venue for weddings and retreats. While historians view destruction as a loss of history and architecture, many within the Black community see it as a form of liberation.  “For a lot of us, it was like our ancestors rising up and fighting back,” Clark shared. “The history isn’t the house; it’s in the records, it’s about the land, it’s about the descendants. It should be a place where people can go and learn.” That concern also shows up in how these stories are covered. Duplessis noted that there is a pattern in the way media portray majority‑Black communities. “When people go to places like the French Quarter, they just see party central.” She explained how news channels and popular media often turn Black suffering and community issues into spectacles. Tanya Mburu, a sophomore nursing major, agreed. “When the news comes to our communities, even our schools, they only show us when we’re in shambles,” she said. “They don’t show when we’re coming together, when we’re doing good things.” Engaging with the rich history of Louisiana requires not only celebrating the resilience of present‑day communities, but looking to the past to honor those who endured and paved the way for them.

item.title: Business as Usual: SU Senate Meeting
item.description: On Monday, Oct. 12, a senate meeting was held in the Smith‑Brown Union to address campus issues, student concerns and provide updates from colleges and campus organizations. The Political Science Department announced a new partnership with the Andrew Goodman Foundation to encourage students to engage more actively in the political climate. Pi Sigma Alpha, the political science honor society, also received a $2,500 grant from the Ty’s Foundation to support its activities and upcoming initiatives. Representatives from Franciscan University’s master’s program and graduate admissions office will meet with psychology students on Oct. 19 to discuss graduate school admission requirements and career opportunities. The department will also offer individual advising sessions to help students review schedules, understand degree requirements and prepare for upcoming semesters. Dates are pending. The School of Nursing has introduced new scholarship opportunities, with one scholarship designated for students at each academic level. The Student Nurse Association will host a breast cancer awareness charity walk on Oct. 26 at 11 a.m. Participants will meet at the nursing building. Pink shirts, $1 ribbons and $25 SU SNA cups will be available. The College of Sciences and Engineering plans to host a town hall meeting with Bio Jags and other organizations, giving students an opportunity to ask questions, share concerns and provide feedback directly to student leaders. Dean Martin announced that a new advising model is in development. Under the proposed model, students would be paired with an advocacy adviser from their department who would support them through graduation. Mental Health Week is planned for the week of Oct. 19. The initiative will focus on student‑athlete well‑being through activities centered on stress management and self‑care. Student‑athletes can attend therapy sessions with Ms. Calhoun on Tuesdays as the department works to expand counseling availability throughout the week. The I.T. Department acknowledged ongoing connectivity issues across campus, particularly in residence halls where cellular coverage is limited or unavailable. Updates will be provided as they become available. Traffic and Parking announced that Mayberry Lot 105, previously reserved for faculty, is now open to students. Priority registration for the spring 2027 semester begins Oct. 19. Students are encouraged to meet with their academic advisers to review degree requirements and ensure they remain on track for graduation. The Senate also addressed a bill proposing changes to student‑assessed fees, including the student union fee. The measure would reduce the fee from $150 to $0 by reversing a previous allocation that directed student fees toward construction of a new student union. If enacted, the change would take effect in spring 2027 and remain in place for at least 30 years. These announcements reflect ongoing efforts across Southern University to expand student opportunities, address campus concerns and improve academic and campus life.

item.title: SU Board Moves Forward on Lab School Build, Electrical System Repairs
item.description: The Southern University Board of Supervisors convened its committee meetings on October 16,  at 9 a.m., opening the morning with student recognition, academic updates, and detailed reports on major campus infrastructure projects. The session began with a call from Mr. Ken Dawson, who reminded members that they are “stewards of a great legacy entrusted with the responsibility of preserving its foundation while preparing it for future generations”. Board members then recognized Southern University Laboratory School senior Jamaia “JC” Kane, praising her academic record, athletic achievements and leadership. Kane told the board her team is prepared to secure another state basketball title, saying “we all have one goal and it’s to win another state championship and bring it back to the lab school.” The board also celebrated the Southern MBA team’s third‑place finish at the National Black MBA Association Case Competition in Los Angeles. Students Rodney Shepard, Megan Abraham and Morgan Abraham were recognized for producing a full pitch deck, conducting competitor analysis and advancing through multiple rounds. Shepard explained that the team “produced a pitch deck, analyzed competitors, did data analysis, financials, and advanced against Jackson State and Tennessee State University.” Board members noted that the Abraham twins previously earned $25,000 each through the Moguls in the Making program. The undergraduate Nexus Louisiana Dev Day team presented its first place project, becoming the first HBCU group to win the competition. Student Jana Pink described their cancer‑support app, Tomorrow, which includes features such as a “hope score” to track patient well‑being and a “legacy vault” for preserving meaningful messages for loved ones. Team member John Hart told the board he is “building the app from the ground up, doing the code and the back end, as well as the front end.” During the Academic Affairs Committee meeting, members approved of the Southern University Laboratory School Faculty and Staff Certification Initiative. Officials also reported that construction drawings for the new lab school should be completed before the next legislative session, with hopes to begin building “sometime late next year” pending state funding. In the Facilities and Property Committee meeting, Dawson delivered a detailed update on campus electrical upgrades. He announced that the temporary switch gear installation was successful, noting “the flow of power is placed in the direction that it was designed for.” He added that $1.5 million in deferred maintenance funds has been redirected to replace failed transformers and switches, and that a comprehensive 14‑week campus power study is underway. Dawson also confirmed that the new business building is moving forward, with bid openings scheduled for November 10.

item.title: SU Presidential Search Committee Names Finalists
item.description: The Southern University System Presidential Search Committee advanced three candidates to the finalist stage Friday after a full morning of semifinalist interviews inside the Board Meeting Room of the J.S. Clark Administration Building. The decision forces the months long national search into its final phase, with the Board of Supervisors expected to vote on the next president in the coming weeks. Committee Chair Ann Smith opened the meeting with roll call and adoption of the agenda before members began interviews with six semifinalists: Dr. Brian Bridges, Dr. Jaffus Hardrick, Atty. Roscoe Jones, Dr. Willie Smith, Dr. Larissa Littleton‑Steib, and Atty. John Belton. Candidates were questioned on leadership experience, student success strategies, and plans for strengthening the nation’s only historically Black university system. Smith emphasized the weight of the moment, saying, “We’re looking for someone who can lead this system forward with vision and stability. This is a critical moment for Southern University.” Throughout the interviews, candidates outlined priorities ranging from enrollment growth to campus infrastructure improvements. Several emphasized expanding academic programs and improving retention across the system’s five campuses. Hardrick highlighted the importance of academic support, stating, “Student success is at the heart of everything we do,” a sentiment that reflected the broader focus of the day’s discussions. After completing interviews and entering executive deliberations, the committee voted to advance three finalists: Dr. Brian Bridges, Dr. Jaffus Hardrick, and Atty. Roscoe Jones. The finalists will participate in additional public sessions and meetings with campus stakeholders before the Board of Supervisors selects the next president. Smith said the committee remains committed to choosing a leader who can guide the system’s long‑term growth. “This is a historic decision for the Southern University System,” she said. “We’re committed to choosing the leader who will best serve our students, faculty, alumni, and the state of Louisiana.” The Board is expected to announce the date of the final vote soon.

item.title: Under the Stars: The Coronation of the 96th Miss Southern
item.description: The crown has officially found its queen. On Wednesday, September 30, the Felton G. Clark Activity Center was transformed into a night of elegance, celebration, and Southern pride for the coronation of Kampbell E. Mack, the 96th Miss Southern University and Agricultural & Mechanical College. With doors opening at 6:30 p.m. and the program beginning at 7 p.m., guests gathered to witness a new chapter in Southern’s royal legacy. The evening opened with a compelling performance by the Southern University Dance Department, whose graceful execution set the tone for the ceremony. “The dancers did well as always. I enjoyed the performance, it was impeccable. The stargazing aesthetic and the music selection helped push the theme and entertain everyone supporting Kampbell,” said Southern University student Taelah Campbell. Following the performance, introductions honored the parents, mentors, royal courts, advisors, and educational leaders who supported Mack throughout her journey. Each acknowledgment highlighted the foundation behind her achievement and the legacies that paved the way. What was once a dream has now blossomed into royalty. As the ceremony continued, anticipation filled the room as she made her entrance, her presence reflecting the elegance and pride of Southern University and A&M College.  “My coronation felt so surreal, it felt like a dream come true. Knowing that I am a part of a legacy that is bigger than me and representing something so much greater than myself means so much to me. It is the best ending to my Southern journey that I could ask for,” Mack said. The legacy of Miss Southern, both past and present, embodies grace, poise, beauty, and intellect. With her hard work culminating in this moment, the 96th Miss Southern University and A&M College were officially crowned by the 95th Miss Southern, Gala J. Marcus and Mack’s advisor, Gabriel S. King, assisted throughout the ceremony. As she leaves her mark on the University, gracefully draped in white, Mack stepped into her reign, proving that at Southern, the crown isn’t just worn, it is earned. “The coronation was a beautiful event. The committee and I spent weeks planning, and it was amazing to see our vision and Miss Southern’s vision truly come to life,” King said. To close the night, the royal court performed a ballroom routine. As the queens received their crowns and photos were taken, the evening under the stars came to an end. “Coronation night was a night to remember. Being surrounded by students, staff, faculty, friends, family, and alumni from beginning to end was amazing. I am officially crowned under the stars,” Mack said. The coronation of Kampbell E. item.title: Gala on the Bluff gives Southern students a seat at the table
item.description: Blue balloons rose along the entrance of L’Auberge Casino & Hotel Baton Rouge as guests covered in blue sparkles made their way into Southern University’s 24th annual Gala on the Bluff. The College of Business was raising money for student scholarships. But the gala also placed students in a room with alumni, business leaders and other professionals, giving them opportunities to make connections beyond campus. “We’re trying to teach them how to be leaders,” said Donald R. Andrews, dean of Southern’s College of Business.  The college hoped to raise at least $125,000 during the event, Andrews said. The Gala on the Bluff was created by members of the College of Business Advisory Council in 2002 to raise funds for scholarships  and build awareness of the college. Now in its 24th year, the gala has provided students with more than $1.5 million in scholarship support, according to the Gala on the Bluff website. The College of Business Advisory Council, chaired by Sharon Hill, also supports the college through fundraising, networking and professional development opportunities for students. Scholarship recipients must be in good academic standing, maintain at least a 2.7 GPA and submit an essay as part of the application process. A committee reviews the applications before recipients are selected. But the college’s goals extend beyond financial assistance. For Southern sophomore Caluntay Jackson, a business management student, the gala was an opportunity to put that idea into practice. Jackson was invited to attend by his professor, Mr. Jones, after a luncheon. He was encouraged to help invite guests and distribute tickets, giving him a chance to take on a leadership role before the event started. He didn’t know what to expect but to show up in a suit and tie. Jackson says it meant everything to him to be invited to the gala, meet important people, and have good energy.  Jackson said students should act when opportunities are presented to them, talk with their professors and remain open to being in professional spaces. “Being seen, just being present is enough,” Jackson said. The gala also highlighted students who have already benefited from the College of Business’ scholarship support. Poster boards throughout the event featured testimonials from 10 scholarship recipients about how the financial assistance affected their college experiences. Among the scholarship recipients featured on the boards was business management student Pharoh Hooks, whose testimonial described how the financial support helped him focus on his studies, campus involvement and professional development. The gala was co-sponsored by Agnes Andrews Allstate Insurance Agency, a longtime partner of the College of Business. The event also brought alumni back into the room. Chauna Banks, a Southern graduate  of 91,’ has attended every Gala on the Bluff  since the event started more than 20 years ago. She remembers when the event was held on Southern’s campus in the Cotillion Ballroom before moving to other venues and eventually to L’Auberge. Banks said she continued attending because the gala was one of the few major events taking place on the Bluff. Six of her aunts and uncles were first-generation college students and regular supporters of the gala, purchasing tables for the event, she said. For Banks, the gala represents the kind of experience that can shape what predominantly Black students see as possible for themselves. “I believe that you start to change the trajectory of your entire family for generations,” Banks said. The College of Business continues to build opportunities that extend beyond the classroom.  As the evening continued, the New Orleans band Royal Essence performed, “ where them fans at”, bringing guests to their feet and filling the room with celebration. The sound of the drums and guitar carried through the ballroom as guests clapped along, their drink glasses vibrating against the tables with each burst of applause. For sophomore Caluntay Jackson, that future starts with the connections he is making now. “Maybe one day, somebody will remember you, give you that job that you wanted,” Jackson said. “Or remember you and they’ll remember your kids too.”

item.title: Southern University Hosts Ecumenical Worship Service Focused on Faith Through Trials
item.description: Southern University and A&M College gathered students, faculty and members of the university community for a morning of worship, music and reflection during the Ecumenical Worship Service on Monday, Sept. 28, at the F.G. Clark Activity Center. The service included Bishop Joseph W. Walker III, presiding bishop of the Full Gospel Baptist Church Fellowship, as the guest speaker and gospel singer Chrystal Rucker as the guest singer. The event focused on faith, perseverance and keeping focus on God during difficult seasons. Walker used the story of Peter walking on water to encourage attendees to remain focused on God during their personal journeys. He described believers as “water walkers,” referencing the moment in Matthew 14 when Peter stepped out of the boat and walked toward Jesus on the water. Walker explained that when people begin a journey with God, challenges and trials may not appear immediately. Instead, they often experience the excitement and positive feelings that come with starting something new. However, when difficulties eventually arise, it can become easy to lose focus. The story of Peter served as an example of what can happen when a person takes their eyes off God. Peter was able to walk on water while his attention remained fixed on Jesus, but he began to sink when he became distracted by the wind and waves around him. Although a university faculty or staff member was not available for an interview about the event, the service still drew participation from students. The atmosphere was filled with worship, music and expressions of faith, with attendees describing a strong spiritual presence throughout the room. For students in the university’s gospel choir, the service provided an opportunity to participate in worship through music. Sophomore Ariell Coates, a member of the gospel choir, said being involved in the service gave her a different perspective. “Being in the gospel choir made me have a perspective on the service. I was the one to entertain, and it was super fun,” Coates said. Senior Jaylia Reed said she expected a strong turnout but was still surprised by the response from attendees. “I expected it to be a turnout, but it was still better than what I expected,” Reed said. “The speaker had everyone’s attention the whole time, and it was overall a good event.” The combination of worship, music and Walker’s message created an atmosphere that emphasized the importance of maintaining faith during difficult moments. For attendees, the service served as a reminder that even when trials arise, keeping their eyes on God can help them move forward.

item.title: First Choice: A Lawyer Leader’s Journey to SULC
item.description: October 06, 2026    Hard work and resilience are deeply rooted in Makayla Delmore’s story. As a student at Southern University Law Center (SULC), Delmore has never settled for anything less than excellence. From an early age, she sought opportunities that would challenge her to grow academically, personally, and professionally. Inspired by her father’s legacy and motivated by academic distinction, Delmore chose SULC as her first-choice law school. She saw the Law Center as the ideal place to continue building upon the foundation she established years earlier through the Early College Option (ECO) program. Offered through the Ascension Parish School Board, the ECO program provided Delmore with the opportunity to earn both a high school diploma and an associate’s degree upon graduation. The experience helped shape her into a solution-oriented, open-minded, and critical thinker skills that would continue to guide her academic journey. “I encourage other students to strive for excellence but also be open to making mistakes, as life's obstacles are overcome through our resilience,” says Delmore. “By completing most of my undergraduate studies prior, my transition to Southeastern Louisiana University was a feat that required me to adjust to a new environment at such a young age." Delmore took those skills she gained from the ECO program to Southeastern Louisiana University, where she acquired a Bachelor of Arts in Criminal Justice. During her undergraduate career, she maintained a 4.0 grade point average and was recognized with the Southeastern President’s Medal for her academic achievement. With her sights set on a career in law, Delmore knew her next step would be choosing a law school that would challenge her. SULC provided the environment she was seeking as she pursued her goal of becoming a lawyer and serving others. Delmore will be the first lawyer in her family of health professionals and military veterans. She plans to use her knowledge and skills to serve those in her community. At Southern University Law Center, every student’s journey is unique. Each student brings their own story, background and experiences that shape their path to becoming a Lawyer Leader. Through the opportunities available at SULC, students are empowered to build on their experiences, pursue their goals and prepare for meaningful careers in the legal profession.

item.title: BUGs National Conference Participants Tour the SU Ag Center’s Demonstration Farm
item.description: Baton Rouge, La. – Thirty-eight Black Farmers & Urban Gardeners (BUGs) National Conference participants visited the Southern University Ag Center’s Demonstration Farm and Research Fields on Oct. 23, 2026. The visit was one of several farm tours offered to the conference’s participants. Dr. Calvin Walker, Executive Vice Chancellor and Professor of Animal Science, greeted the group and Dr. Tiffany Franklin, Vice Chancellor for Extension & Outreach, officially welcomed the participants to the Southern University Ag Center’s Demonstration Farm. Members of the SU Ag Center’s Agriculture and Natural Resource (ANR) team served as guides during the walking tour. Pamela James, a BUGs participant from Buffalo, New York said she selected the SU AgCenter’s tour to see what type of farm operations and research were being conducted that she could learn more about and bring back to her classes and her organization, Life Source Systems, Inc. James, who is a professor at Houghton University and serves as the CEO of Life Source Systems, was intrigued by the Ag Center’s hemp research.   “One of the tour guides was talking about the hemp plant and how it can dry up and the THC could not be as potent because of it being left there in the sun too long,” explained James. “I have never heard that before and that’s interesting because when it’s sold a lot of times people think just because it’s grown, they are getting the full potency but it depends on who grew it and where it was grown, how long it was grown, and how long it stayed in the ground, so that was something different,” she added. The BUGs National Conference is the largest urban grower’s conference in America. The conference is being held from Oct. 23 – 25, 2026 in New Orleans at Dillard University. It is committed to building a strong community to support growers who cultivate in both urban and rural settings by providing a space for attendees to learn, network, and discuss ways to advance their growth and success in agriculture businesses. For additional information about the SU Ag Center’s Demonstration Farm or upcoming programs, contact Stephanie Elwood at stephanie_elwood@suagcenter.com.

item.title: National Science Foundation Project on Tire-Wear Pollution Strengthens Southern University & Grambling State University’s Research and STEM Training Partnership
item.description: When many people think about Southern University and Grambling State University the annual Bayou Classic football game in New Orleans usually comes to mind, but the two colleges have been collaborating off the grid iron as well.  One of these collaborations is a National Science Foundation (NSF) research project focused on the emerging environmental impacts of tire-wear pollution. Southern University’s Department of Environmental Toxicology in the College of Agricultural, Human and Environmental Sciences (CAHES) received $893,779 in funding for the collaborative research project with Grambling State University (GSU) to advance fundamental environmental science while expanding interdisciplinary research and STEM training opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students. The research focuses on 6-PPD quinone (6-PPDQ), a transformation product of 6-PPD, a chemical widely used in automobile tires. Tire wear releases these chemicals into the environment, and 6-PPDQ has emerged as a contaminant of growing concern due to its widespread occurrence and documented biological effects. Despite increasing recognition of this emerging contaminant, the fundamental molecular mechanisms through which 6-PPDQ affects cellular function remain incompletely understood. The Southern University-Grambling State University research team will investigate how 6-PPDQ disrupts the molecular processes that allow cells to respond and adapt to environmental stress. Particular emphasis will be placed on interactions among stress granules and processing bodies, which regulate RNA processing during cellular stress, and Polycomb repressive complexes, which regulate gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. Using human lung epithelial cells, the investigators will integrate advanced molecular biology, high-resolution imaging, transcriptomics, proteomics, and computational approaches, including molecular modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and density functional theory, to determine how the environmental contaminant perturbs interconnected RNA-regulatory and epigenetic networks. The research is expected to generate fundamental knowledge and broadly applicable experimental and computational approaches for understanding the molecular actions of emerging environmental contaminants. The project represents an expansion of an established research and student-training collaboration between Southern University and Grambling State University. Undergraduate students from GSU will engage directly in project-related researchand receive hands-on training in environmental toxicology, molecular and cellular biology, advanced imaging, transcriptomic and proteomic approaches, computational modeling, and data analysis. Students will work closely with Southern University faculty and doctoral trainees, creating an interdisciplinary environment where undergraduate researchers can develop technical expertise, critical-thinking abilities, scientific communication skills, and greater confidence as emerging scientists. The project will also provide important professional development opportunities for Southern University doctoral students, who will participate in training and near-peer mentoring of GSU undergraduate researchers. This multi-level mentoring approach will simultaneously provide undergraduate students with access to research mentors and enable doctoral trainees to develop leadership, teaching, and mentoring skills that are increasingly important for careers in academia, biotechnology, industry, and government. An important long-term goal of the collaboration is to strengthen an undergraduate-to-doctoral STEM pathway between Grambling State University and Southern University. By providing GSU students with sustained research experiences, faculty, and graduate-student mentoring, exposure to advanced research technologies, and familiarity with Southern University’s doctoral training environment, the project will encourage talented undergraduate students to consider advanced education, including doctoral training in Environmental Toxicology at Southern University. The project will further extend its educational impact through K–12 STEM outreach activities designed to introduce younger students to environmental science, toxicology, biotechnology, and computational research. Dr. Sanjay Batra, Professor and Chair of the Department of Environmental Toxicology, serves as the Principal Investigator (PI) of the project and Dr. Waneene Dorsey, the Ernest Everett Just Endowed Professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at Grambling State University, serves as Co-Principal Investigator(Co-PI). The project began in September 2026 and will conclude in August 2029. ‍
